procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 14 May 2009 passed by the learned District Judge, Kamrup, Gauhati in M.A Case No. 18/2008
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Gauhati High Court allowed a Civil Revision Petition (CRP No. 263 of 2009 dated 21 July 2011) against the order of the District Judge.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellants assailed the judgement of the Gauhati High Court passed in CRP No. 263 of 2009 dated 21 July 2011. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal and restored the file to the docket of the concerned District Judge for him to proceed in accordance with law.

directions: The file is restored to the docket of the concerned District Judge for him to proceed in accordance with law and in light of the discussions made herein.

The same be decided possibly within a period of three months from the date on which a copy of this judgment and order is received by the District Judge, as is necessitated by the attending facts and circumstances.

issue.issue_text: Whether Article 116 of the Limitation Act 1963, applies to proceedings under the Jogighopa (Assam) Unit of Ashok Paper Mills Limited (Acquisition Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1990 and; if the Limitation Act does not apply then, in the absence of Limitation being placed within the text of the Statute in question, could the Appeal filed against the Order of the Commissioner of Payments be held as maintainable having been filed after a period of nearly three years from the said order.

facts: An appeal was filed against an order of the Commissioner of Payments, nearly three years after the order was passed.
The appeal was filed under the Jogighopa (Assam) Unit of Ashok Paper Mills Limited (Acquisition Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1990 (the "Jogighopa Act").
The Jogighopa Act itself does not specify a time limit for filing such an appeal.

law.description: This article prescribes the period of limitation for filing an appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC).

law.law_name: Jogighopa (Assam) Unit of Ashok Paper Mills Limited (Acquisition Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1990
law.description: A special statute that provides for an appeal from the Commissioner of Payments to the High Court but does not prescribe a limitation period. It limits the application of the CPC to certain specific aspects only.
A legal principle holding that when a statute does not prescribe a time limit for performing an act, that act must be performed within a reasonable time.

application.description: The Court first addressed whether Article 116 of the Limitation Act applied. It concluded that it did not.
application.reasoning: The Court reasoned that an appeal under the Jogighopa Act is not an appeal under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC). The Assam Legislature had intentionally limited the application of the CPC to very specific and narrow purposes within the Jogighopa Act. Therefore, the limitation period prescribed in Article 116 for CPC appeals was not applicable.

application.description: The Court highlighted the unique (*sui generis*) nature of the appeal procedure under the Jogighopa Act.
application.reasoning: The fact that the Act allows a High Court Judge to be the Commissioner of Payments and provides for an appeal from that order to a Division Bench of the High Court further demonstrated that the appeal process was distinct from the standard procedures governed by the CPC.

application.description: Having found the Limitation Act inapplicable, the Court considered whether the appeal could be filed at any time.
application.reasoning: The Court rejected the idea of an indefinite right to appeal. It held that in the absence of a statutorily prescribed limitation period, the principle of 'reasonable time' must be applied. This means an appeal must be filed within a time that is reasonable under the circumstances of the case.

application.description: The Court then applied the 'reasonable time' principle to the facts of the case.
application.reasoning: The Court noted that while the absence of a limitation period does not permit parties to litigate issues decades later, shorter delays would not necessarily be barred by laches. By accepting the appeal, the Court implicitly found that the delay of nearly three years was within a 'reasonable time' in this specific context.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that Article 116 of the Limitation Act, 1963, does not apply to appeals under the Jogighopa Act, as these are not appeals under the Code of Civil Procedure. In the absence of a specific limitation period in the Jogighopa Act, the Court applied the principle of 'reasonable time' and concluded that the appeal, filed after a delay of nearly three years, was maintainable.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Article 116 of the Limitation Act 1963, applies to proceedings under the Jogighopa (Assam) Unit of Ashok Paper Mills Limited (Acquisition Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1990 and; if the Limitation Act does not apply then, in the absence of Limitation being placed within the text of the Statute in question, could the Appeal filed against the Order of the Commissioner of Payments be held as maintainable having been filed after a period of nearly three years from the said order.
appellant_arguments: The appellants filed an application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1963 to condone the delay, proceeding on the basis that the delay could be excused.
Without prejudice, even if Article 116 of the Limitation Act applies or if the standard is a 'reasonable period', the matter should be remanded to the District Judge.
The District Judge, as the appellate court, should be allowed to consider the application for condonation of delay and determine if there was 'sufficient cause' for it.
respondent_arguments: Courts should not adopt a liberal approach in condoning delays, especially when there is an absence of sufficient cause.

statutes.act_name: Jogighopa (Assam) Unit of Ashok Paper Mills Limited (Acquisition Transfer of Undertaking) Act, 1990

cases.case_name: Vidyacharan Shukla v. Khubchand Baghel & Ors.
cases.principle: Cited to distinguish the present case, as the special law in Vidyacharan Shukla (Representation of People Act, 1951) explicitly provided that the procedure for an appeal would be in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure, which is not the case with the Jogighopa Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a legislature consciously prescribes limitation periods for certain actions within a statute but deliberately omits to prescribe a limitation period for a specific right of appeal, it indicates a legislative intent that no period of limitation is applicable to that specific right.
obiter: The principle of statutory interpretation 'expression unius est exclusio alterius' means the expression of one thing is the exclusion of the other.
The objective of the Law of Limitation is to ensure that a dispute does not survive endlessly and that parties are not left in a state of uncertainty.
Courts should not take a liberal approach in the condonation of delay in the absence of sufficient cause.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a court is faced with a situation where no limitation period is provided by either the specific statute governing the dispute or the general Limitation Act, it is improper for the court to invent a limitation period. Instead, the court must conduct a holistic assessment of the facts and circumstances to determine if the delay has caused prejudice to a party. The dismissal of a plea solely on the ground of delay, without examining the prejudice caused, is incorrect.
legal_tests_applied: In the absence of a prescribed limitation period, a court must undertake a holistic assessment of the facts and circumstances of the case to examine the possibility of delay causing prejudice to a party.
The assessment should consider the conduct of the parties, the nature of the proceeding, the length of the delay, the possibility of prejudice being caused, and the scheme of the statute in question.

When a party raises the defense of delay in a situation where no limitation period is prescribed, that party bears the burden of demonstrating how the delay itself would cause additional prejudice or loss.
Courts should be wary of prescribing a specific period of limitation in cases where the legislature has refrained from doing so.
policy_considerations: It would be inappropriate for a Court to supplant the legislature’s wisdom by its own and provide a limitation, more so in accordance with what it believes to be the appropriate period.

In the absence of a specific limitation, it would be improper for courts to dismiss a plea solely on the ground of delay without having examined the nature of prejudice caused to the other party in the facts and circumstances of the case at hand.

When a statute does not provide for an explicit limitation, the urgency to act with expedition that exists when a limitation period is specified may be absent, and shorter delays would not attract the doctrine of delay and laches.
